title: Steve Jobs — Macworld 2007 Keynote, iPhone Introduction
role: control case / non-pitch rhetorical exemplar (Logos+Ethos-led PRODUCT pitch)

highlights.quote: and we are calling it iPhone.
highlights.note: The naming reveal collapses three separate product categories (widescreen iPod, phone, internet communicator) into one falsifiable product claim, rather than an emotional appeal.

highlights.quote: multi-touch, which is phenomenal. It works like magic.
highlights.note: A mechanism claim for the enabling technology behind the touch interface, immediately followed by a live demo that lets the audience verify it themselves.

highlights.quote: really serious about software should make their own hardware.
highlights.note: Borrows the authority of industry pioneer Alan Kay to justify Apple's integrated hardware-and-software strategy — credibility by association.

highlights.quote: something wonderful for your hand. Just wonderful.
highlights.note: A pure sensory/aesthetic appeal to physical delight in the object, with no functional or evidentiary content.
A third party's spontaneous emotional reaction, quoted back to the audience as social proof of delight rather than as a technical claim.

highlights.quote: how thrilled I am to make the first public phone call with iPhone.
highlights.note: Genuine, unscripted human emotion during a live, high-stakes demo — the risk of the moment itself generates the pathos.
Textbook market-math logos: a quantifiable, independently checkable claim about market opportunity, exactly the kind of arithmetic a skeptical listener could verify.

highlights.quote: I skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it has been.
highlights.note: A closing borrowed-authority quote (Wayne Gretzky) that recasts Apple's history as visionary foresight, sealing the credibility argument on the way out.

summary: This keynote is a logos-and-ethos-led product pitch: most of Jobs's persuasive effort goes into demonstrating mechanism live on stage, drawing feature-by-feature comparisons against existing smartphones, and laying out quantifiable market logic (unit pricing, '1% share = 10 million units'), while ethos is built through Apple's track record (1984 Mac, 2001 iPod), borrowed-authority quotes (Alan Kay, Wayne Gretzky), a stated 200+ patents, and on-stage validation from Google, Yahoo, and Cingular/AT&T executives. Pathos is present but clearly subordinate, and mostly aesthetic or delight-oriented (wonder at the object, a colleague's genuine emotion on the first live call) rather than stakes-based or other-directed. As a control case it shows what these three appeals sound like when there is no 'evidence of impact' or 'scale & sustainability' dimension to satisfy at all: the only 'evidence' needed is that the demo works in front of a live audience, and the only 'sustainability' question is unit economics and carrier distribution — not whether a social outcome persists for the people it is meant to help.
